summary: Adds a way for a softwire client using DHCPv4 over DHCPv6 (RFC 7341) to tell the network which IPv6 address it will use as the source of its IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel. Operators need this for some softwire mechanisms, such as those in RFC 7596 and RFC 7597. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: To deliver old-style mail through a new kind of postal system, the post office needs to know your return address on the new system. This document lets your device tell the network that address.

questions: ipv4 over ipv6 tunnel source address dhcp
how does a softwire client report its ipv6 source address
subtitle: How a softwire client tells its DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 server which IPv6 address it will use as its tunnel source.

tldr.problem: Some IPv4-over-IPv6 softwire mechanisms need the operator to know the IPv6 address the client will use as the source of its tunnel, but DHCP 4o6 had no way to carry it.
tldr.mechanism: A new DHCPv4 option, OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR (109), carries the client's softwire source address to the server, and a new DHCPv6 option, OPTION_S46_BIND_IPV6_PREFIX (137), lets the server hint at a preferred prefix. The server stores the address with the IPv4 lease.
tldr.outcome: The operator can build the binding table entry for the border relay from the server's lease data. The RFC also updates RFC 7598 so that OPTION_S46_BR (90) can be used on its own.

today: RFC 8539 is a Proposed Standard from March 2019 that updates RFC 7598. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: Telling the Operator the Tunnel Source
sections.content:
Deterministic IPv4-over-IPv6 transition technologies need elements preconfigured with binding rules, so the client's softwire source address must use a predetermined prefix, usually configured on the home gateway. RFC 7598 describes a DHCPv6-based mechanism for that deterministic case.

A dynamic model that uses DHCPv4 over DHCPv6 (DHCP 4o6, RFC 7341) allows much more flexibility in where the source address sits. The IPv6 address is sent back to the service provider, so the matching softwire configuration can be created in the border relay (BR). Dynamic allocation also saves IPv4 resources, because only clients that keep renewing their lease hold on to the address.

The mechanism only applies to softwire clients provisioned through DHCP 4o6. The RFC names RFC 7597 and RFC 7596 as softwire technologies suitable for extension with DHCP 4o6 and dynamic IPv4 leasing.
sections.eli5: When your home network borrows a special tunnel to reach the old internet, the company running the tunnel must know which door you are using. This document is how your device tells them.

sections.title: Solution Overview
sections.content:
A softwire needs both IPv6 and IPv4 configuration. The IPv6 part travels in DHCPv6 options inside the DHCPV4-RESPONSE (21) message. OPTION_S46_BR (90) gives the IPv6 address of the softwire BR. OPTION_S46_BIND_IPV6_PREFIX (137) is optionally sent by the server to indicate a preferred IPv6 prefix for binding the IPv4 configuration and sourcing tunnel traffic. That may be needed when the customer network uses several prefixes, such as Unique Local Addresses, or when the transition mechanism requires a particular prefix.

The IPv4 part travels in DHCPv4 messages inside OPTION_DHCPV4_MSG (87), as defined in RFC 7341.

To report the source address, this RFC defines the DHCPv4 option OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR (109). The client puts it in DHCPREQUEST messages, and the server stores it for the lifetime of the IPv4 lease.

RFC 7598 only allowed OPTION_S46_BR inside the container options OPTION_S46_CONT_MAPE (94) or OPTION_S46_CONT_LW (96). This RFC updates it so the option can be listed in the client's Option Request Option (ORO) and appear directly in the server's messages.
sections.eli5: Two kinds of notes travel together. One carries the old-style address, and the other says where the tunnel starts. This RFC adds a new note slot so the child can say where its own end of the tunnel is.

sections.title: The Two New Options
sections.content:
OPTION_S46_BIND_IPV6_PREFIX (137) is a DHCPv6 option. Its option-length is 1 plus the length of the prefix in bytes. The bindprefix6-len field is 8 bits and gives the prefix length in bits, with valid values 0 to 128. The bind-ipv6-prefix field is (bindprefix6-len + 7) / 8 bytes long and is padded on the right with zero bits, which the receiver ignores. It is a singleton, so servers MUST NOT send more than one.

OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR (109) is a DHCPv4 option with an option-length of 16. Its softwire-ipv6-src-address field is 16 bytes: the IPv6 address that is being requested for binding or currently bound to the client's IPv4 configuration.

The RFC explains why the client identifier cannot do this job. The chaddr field and the Client Identifier (61) option must stay constant during a lease, but the client may only be able to build its softwire address after it receives the first DHCPV4-RESPONSE containing OPTION_S46_BIND_IPV6_PREFIX.
sections.eli5: There are two new forms. One lets the company suggest which street your tunnel address should be on. The other lets you write down the exact address you chose.

sections.title: The Message Flow
sections.content:
The exchange rides on the normal DHCP 4o6 allocation, with DHCPv4 messages wrapped in DHCPV4-QUERY (20) or DHCPV4-RESPONSE (21).

  1. The client sends a DHCPV4-QUERY with OPTION_ORO (6) listing 90 and 137, and a DHCPDISCOVER inside OPTION_DHCPV4_MSG.
  2. The server answers with a DHCPV4-RESPONSE containing OPTION_S46_BR (90) with the BR address, optionally OPTION_S46_BIND_IPV6_PREFIX (137), and a DHCPOFFER with an available IPv4 address.
  3. The client sends a DHCPV4-QUERY with a DHCPREQUEST for that IPv4 address, carrying OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR with the IPv6 address it will use as softwire source.
  4. The server sends a DHCPV4-RESPONSE with a DHCPACK that has the allocated IPv4 address and the bound source address in the same option.
sections.eli5: The device asks, the server offers an address and tells where the tunnel goes, the device says which address it picked, and the server repeats it back to confirm.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
Before starting, the client MUST be configured with a suitable IPv6 prefix for the local softwire endpoint, obtained for example by DHCPv6 or Router Advertisement. The client first enables DHCP 4o6 as in RFC 7341. If the offer has no valid OPTION_S46_BR with at least one BR address, the client MUST discard it. If it carries a valid OPTION_S46_BIND_IPV6_PREFIX, the client uses it as the "IPv6 binding prefix" to choose an active prefix, following Section 5.1 of RFC 7596. Otherwise the client MAY pick any valid prefix of suitable scope. It may reuse an existing address or create a new one, and in the latter case MUST finish configuring it, including duplicate address detection if required, first.

On every lease renewal or rebinding, and whenever the IPv6 address changes (for example after renumbering), the client MUST include OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR with its current address in the DHCPREQUEST. If the DHCPACK returns a different address, the client SHOULD wait a randomized interval and resend; the default minimum time is 60 seconds, after which it MAY send DHCPRELEASE and start over. A DHCPNAK means failure and the client restarts from Step 1. A DHCPRELEASE does not carry the option.

The client validates option 137 by checking that bindprefix6-len is not larger than 128 and that the byte count matches. If either check fails, it discards the option and proceeds as if it had not been received.

The server MUST store the client's IPv6 softwire source address in its lease database next to the IPv4 address and client identifier, and MUST send OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR in every DHCPACK. The binding is valid as long as the lease is. If a client changes its address, the server updates it and acknowledges. The server MAY enforce a minimum interval between updates, with a default of 60 seconds, and may silently drop early updates or answer with the existing binding.

Each customer edge's source address must be unique. On every DHCPREQUEST with the option, the server MUST check the address against all other active leases. On a clash it MUST NOT store or update it, and either returns a DHCPNAK (no active lease) or drops the message or returns the existing binding (active lease).
sections.eli5: The device must tell the server its address whenever it renews or changes it. The server keeps a list and makes sure no two devices claim the same address.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7341 also apply. The new risk is a rogue client sending a DHCPREQUEST for another client's active lease with its own softwire address, to redirect that client's IPv4 traffic. To do so it would need the victim's client identifier and active IPv4 lease. The RFC walks through three ways to learn them. Snooping on a shared access medium is why the mechanism is NOT RECOMMENDED there; it is intended for a dedicated Layer 2 access network per client. Snooping in the ISP's core already requires infrastructure access. Brute-force guessing can be made harder with a random-based client identifier (Section 3.5 of RFC 7844).

Redirecting flows to a client that cannot handle them can be countered with network ingress filtering (RFC 2827, BCP 38) plus the BR source address validation of RFC 7596 and RFC 7597. A client flooding the server with address updates can be limited by the minimum update interval from the server behavior rules.

On privacy, the anonymity profiles of RFC 7844 also apply. A fixed interface identifier in the softwire source address could make a device trackable across networks. Building the address as in Section 6 of RFC 7597 avoids this, because the identifier then contains only the allocated IPv4 address (and the port set identifier if RFC 7618 is used), so it changes when the IPv4 address does.
sections.eli5: A sneaky device might try to grab someone else's mail by pretending to be them. The fixes are to keep neighbors from listening in, use hard-to-guess names, and avoid labels that follow you around.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned option code 137 for OPTION_S46_BIND_IPV6_PREFIX in the DHCPv6 Option Codes registry, with Client ORO set to Yes and Singleton Option set to Yes. It also assigned tag 109 for OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR in the BOOTP Vendor Extensions and DHCP Options registry, with data length 16.

The entry for OPTION_S46_BR (90) changed its Client ORO value from No to Yes, and its reference now lists both RFC 7598 and RFC 8539.
sections.eli5: The official option list got two new entries and one old entry was edited, so everyone uses the same numbers.

messages.label: DHCPV4-RESPONSE: DHCPOFFER
messages.note: Carries OPTION_S46_BR (90), optionally 137, and an available IPv4 address.

messages.label: DHCPV4-QUERY: DHCPREQUEST
messages.note: Includes OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR (109) with the softwire source address.

messages.label: DHCPV4-RESPONSE: DHCPACK
messages.note: Leased IPv4 address plus the bound source address in option 109.

items.label: OPTION_S46_BR
items.desc: DHCPv6: BR IPv6 address; may now appear without a container option.

items.label: OPTION_S46_BIND_IPV6_PREFIX
items.desc: DHCPv6: preferred prefix to bind IPv4 configuration to.

items.label: OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR
items.desc: DHCPv4: the client's softwire IPv6 source address, 16 bytes.

items.label: OPTION_DHCPV4_MSG
items.desc: DHCPv6: carries an encapsulated DHCPv4 message.
